q: Electricity is a form of ____.
e: Electricity is fundamentally defined as a form of energy that can be transformed into other forms.

q: There are two types of electricity: electrostatics (or) static electricity and ____ (or) current electricity.
e: Electrodynamics is the study of moving electric charges and their interaction with magnetic and electric fields.

q: Electrostatics is the study of electric charge at ____.
e: Electrostatics specifically deals with stationary electric charges, as opposed to moving charges.

q: Electrodynamics is the study of moving electric charges and their interaction with magnetic and ____ fields.
e: Moving charges interact with both magnetic and electric fields, which is the focus of electrodynamics.

q: Electric charge is the physical property of matter that causes an electric force when placed in an ____ field.
e: An electromagnetic field is the physical field produced by electrically charged objects.

q: Electric charges may be either at rest (static charges) or in ____ (moving charges).
e: Charges can exist in a static state or be in motion, the latter of which constitutes an electric current.

q: Flow of charges is called an electric ____.
e: An electric current is defined as the rate of flow of electric charge through a conductor.

q: A French scientist, ____, studied the nature of electric charges possessed by substances and found that there were only two kinds of charges.
e: Du Fay was an early researcher who identified the existence of two distinct types of electric charges.

q: Benjamin Franklin named them positive charge which is represented by a plus sign (+) and negative charge by a ____ sign (-).
e: Benjamin Franklin established the convention of using plus and minus signs to denote positive and negative charges.

q: Like charges ____ and unlike charges attract.
e: This is a fundamental law of electrostatics: charges of the same sign push each other away.

q: The closer the charges are, the ____ the force between them.
e: The electric force is inversely related to the distance between the charges, increasing as they get closer.

q: When two charged objects are brought together, they produce either attractive or ____ force.
e: Depending on whether the charges are unlike or like, the resulting force will be attractive or repulsive.

q: The electric force between two charged objects is one of the ____ forces of nature.
e: The electric force is one of the four fundamental forces that govern interactions in the universe.

q: The electric force holds the particles that make up an ____ together.
e: The attractive electric force between the positive nucleus and negative electrons binds the atom together.

q: Charged objects can exert forces to other charged objects without being in ____ with them.
e: Electric force is a non-contact force, meaning it can act over a distance.

q: This is possible because there is an electric ____ around each charge.
e: An electric field is the region around a charged particle where a force would be exerted on other charged particles.

q: In SI units, electric charge is measured in ____ (C), in honour of Charles Augustin de Coulomb, a French physicist.
e: The coulomb is the standard SI unit for measuring the quantity of electric charge.

q: He discovered that the force between two charged objects depends on the magnitude of their charges and on how ____ apart they are.
e: Coulomb's law states that the force is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.

q: Since the magnitude of charge of an electron is $1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C, one coulomb of charge is equivalent to the charge of ____ electrons.
e: One coulomb is a relatively large amount of charge, equal to the combined charge of approximately $6.25 \times 10^{18}$ electrons.

q: One microcoulomb ($1 \mu\text{C}$) = ____ C (one millionth of a coulomb).
e: The prefix 'micro' denotes a factor of $10^{-6}$, making a microcoulomb one millionth of a coulomb.

q: Charge is one of the ____ physical quantities.
e: Quantization means that charge exists only in discrete, indivisible packets rather than continuous values.

q: It means that charge cannot take any arbitrary values, but only discrete values that are integral multiples of the fundamental charge that is charge of an ____.
e: The elementary charge, carried by a single electron, is the smallest observable unit of free electric charge.

q: The formula for quantized charge is $Q = ne$, where $Q$ = electric charge, $n$ = ____, $e$ = charge of an electron.
e: In the quantization formula, $n$ must be a whole number, representing the count of elementary charges.

q: Matter is composed of ____ which are very small in size.
e: Atoms are the basic building blocks of all ordinary matter.

q: An atom consists of a core called the ____ around which the particles called electrons are moving in orbits.
e: The nucleus is the dense, central region of an atom containing protons and neutrons.

q: An electron is a negatively charged particle having a charge of ____ C.
e: The electron carries a fundamental negative charge of exactly $-1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ coulombs.

q: The nucleus consists of two kinds of particles called proton and ____.
e: Protons and neutrons are the two types of nucleons that make up the atomic nucleus.

q: A proton is a positively charged particle and a neutron is an ____ particle.
e: Neutrons are electrically neutral, meaning they have no net electric charge.

q: An electron and a proton have the same ____ of electric charge.
e: Although their signs are opposite, the absolute value of the charge of an electron and a proton is identical.

q: The nucleus has net ____ charge.
e: Because the nucleus contains positively charged protons and neutral neutrons, its overall charge is positive.

q: The magnitude of positive charge of the nucleus is equal to the sum of the positive charges of all the protons present in the ____.
e: The total positive charge of the nucleus is determined solely by the number of protons it contains.

q: In a normal atom the number of orbiting electrons is always equal to the number of ____.
e: This balance ensures that the atom as a whole has no net electric charge.

q: Since the magnitude of positive charge of the nucleus is equal to that of the total negative charge of electrons, a normal atom has no ____ charge.
e: The equal and opposite charges cancel each other out, resulting in a net charge of zero.

q: It is said to be electrically ____.
e: An atom with equal numbers of protons and electrons is electrically neutral.

q: If an atom gains one or more electrons, it carries a ____ charge.
e: Gaining negatively charged electrons gives the atom an overall negative charge.

q: If an atom loses one or more electrons, it becomes ____ charged.
e: Losing negative electrons leaves the atom with an excess of positive protons, making it positively charged.

q: When an atom becomes a charged atom, it is called an ____.
e: An ion is an atom or molecule that has a net electrical charge due to the loss or gain of electrons.

q: In an atom the negatively charged electrons are moving around a ____ charged nucleus.
e: The nucleus is positively charged due to the presence of protons.

q: Some of these electrons are near the nucleus while other electrons are further ____ from the nucleus.
e: Electrons occupy different energy levels or orbits at varying distances from the nucleus.

q: Since positive and negative charges attract each other, electrons experience an ____ force of the nucleus.
e: The opposite charges of the nucleus and electrons create an attractive electrostatic force.

q: As the attractive force is greater for the electrons closer to the nucleus so these electrons cannot move ____.
e: Strong attraction to the nucleus restricts the movement of inner electrons.

q: The electrons closer to the nucleus are called ____ electrons.
e: Bound electrons are tightly held by the nucleus and cannot easily leave the atom.

q: The electrons far away from the nucleus (or) the outer electrons experience less attractive force of the ____.
e: The attractive force weakens with distance, affecting outer electrons less strongly.

q: This means that the outer electrons are loosely bound and are called ____ electrons.
e: Free electrons are not tightly bound to any specific atom and can move through a material.

q: They can move from one ____ to another.
e: The ability of free electrons to move between atoms is what allows for electrical conduction.

q: The number of free electrons in a substance depends upon the ____ of that substance.
e: The atomic structure and bonding of a material determine how many free electrons it has.

q: The substance which has plenty of free electrons is called a ____ and the substance which has very few (or) no free electrons is called an insulator.
e: Conductors are characterized by an abundance of free electrons that facilitate the flow of electric current.

q: Metals are good electrical ____.
e: Metals have a 'sea of free electrons' that makes them highly effective at conducting electricity.

q: Some of their electrons are so loosely held to their atoms that they can pass ____ from atom to atom.
e: This free movement of electrons is the defining characteristic of metallic conduction.

q: Most non-metals conduct electricity poorly or not at all, although ____ is an exception.
e: Carbon, particularly in its graphite form, has delocalized electrons that allow it to conduct electricity.

q: In insulators all the electrons are held tightly in position and unable to move from atom to ____.
e: The lack of mobile charge carriers is why insulators resist the flow of electric current.

q: Insulators are materials that hardly conduct ____.
e: Insulators are used to prevent the unwanted flow of electrical current.

q: Although the electrons are not free to move in insulators, they can be ____ from one object to another.
e: Insulators can still be charged by friction, which involves the transfer of electrons on their surface.

q: Some substances which contain a moderate amount of free electrons are called ____.
e: Semiconductors have electrical conductivity between that of a conductor and an insulator.

q: Such substances are neither conductors nor ____.
e: Semiconductors occupy a middle ground, and their conductivity can be precisely controlled.

q: Silicon and ____ are widely used as semiconductors.
e: Silicon and germanium are the two most common elemental semiconductors used in electronics.

q: Metals such as gold, silver, copper, brass, aluminium etc., are good ____.
e: These metals are frequently used in wiring and electrical components due to their high conductivity.

q: Non-metals such as plastic, glass, rubber, wax, quartz, etc., are ____.
e: These materials are commonly used to coat or separate electrical conductors to prevent short circuits.

q: Transistors and other electronic components are made from ____.
e: The controlled conductivity of semiconductors is the foundation of modern solid-state electronics.

q: Normally, atoms have equal numbers of electrons and protons so the net (overall) charge on a material is ____.
e: In an uncharged state, the positive and negative charges within a material perfectly balance each other.

q: However, when the two insulating materials are rubbed together, electrons may be ____ from one to the other.
e: Friction between insulators can cause electrons to be stripped from one material and deposited onto the other.

q: If two uncharged objects are rubbed with one another both of them become ____.
e: The transfer of electrons results in one object gaining a net positive charge and the other a net negative charge.

q: This is also called charging by ____.
e: Charging by friction is the process of generating static electricity through the rubbing of two different materials.

q: It is important that the rubbing does not produce or create charges but removes electrons from one object and ____ them to the other.
e: This aligns with the law of conservation of charge; charge is neither created nor destroyed, only moved.

q: As shown when a glass rod is rubbed with a silk cloth, the glass rod becomes ____ charged and the silk cloth negatively charged.
e: Glass tends to lose electrons to silk, leaving the glass rod with a net positive charge.

q: This is because some electrons of the glass rod are transferred to the ____ cloth.
e: The silk cloth gains the electrons lost by the glass, acquiring a net negative charge.

q: Hence, the glass rod loses electrons while the silk cloth ____ electrons.
e: The loss of negative electrons results in a positive charge, while the gain results in a negative charge.

q: As another example, when a plastic rod is rubbed with fur, the plastic rod possesses a negative charge while the fur becomes ____ charged.
e: Plastic tends to gain electrons from fur, leaving the fur with a deficit of electrons and thus a positive charge.

q: Induction is the process of charging a conductor without any ____ with the charged body.
e: Charging by induction uses the electric field of a charged object to redistribute charges in a neutral conductor.

q: A charged object can attract ____ objects.
e: A charged object can induce a temporary charge separation in an uncharged object, leading to attraction.

q: The law of conservation of electric charge is one of the ____ laws.
e: This law states that the total electric charge in an isolated system remains constant over time.

q: That is 'The net electric charge in an isolated system remains ____'.
e: Charge cannot be created or destroyed, so the total net charge of an isolated system does not change.

q: The net charge is the ____ sum of the charges in an isolated system.
e: The net charge is calculated by adding positive and negative charges together, taking their signs into account.

q: For example, in the experiment on electrification by stroking the glass rod with a silk cloth, they together form an ____ system.
e: Assuming no charge is lost to the surroundings, the rod and cloth together conserve the total charge.

q: There is no charge transfer between the surrounding and the ____ system.
e: By definition, an isolated system does not exchange matter or charge with its environment.

q: The net charge of isolated system remains constant before and after ____.
e: The act of rubbing or stroking only redistributes the existing charge between the two objects.

q: There are several practical uses of static electricity in our daily ____.
e: Static electricity is harnessed in various common technologies and industrial applications.

q: Photocopier, electrostatic paint spraying, electrostatic precipitator etc., are based on static electric ____.
e: These applications rely on the attractive and repulsive forces between static electric charges.

q: Basic operation of a photocopier is the attraction of charged toner (ink) to the region on the selenium coated drum that is ____ charged.
e: Opposite charges attract, allowing the toner to stick precisely to the charged image areas on the drum.

q: The item to be painted receives the negative charge from a negatively charged ____.
e: In electrostatic paint spraying, the target object is grounded or connected to a negative electrode.

q: The droplets of paint emerge from the spray gun are ____ charged.
e: The paint droplets are given a positive charge so they are attracted to the negatively charged object.

q: As the droplets all carry the same charge they repel and spread out forming a fine ____.
e: Mutual repulsion between the positively charged droplets prevents them from clumping together.

q: The paint droplets are attracted to the surface of the ____.
e: The electrostatic attraction ensures the paint wraps around and adheres evenly to the metal frame.

q: The paint is attracted statically to metal frame from every direction so there is no ____ of spray paint.
e: This method is highly efficient, minimizing overspray and reducing material waste.

q: The waste smoke, dust and fly ash are passed through a negatively charged mesh of wire in the chimney and the fly ash particles become ____ charged.
e: As the particles pass the charged mesh, they acquire a negative charge through induction or conduction.

q: Higher up the chimney these charged particles are attracted and stick to positively charged metal ____.
e: The negatively charged ash is drawn to the positively charged collecting plates, removing it from the smoke.

q: The clean smoke is then released into the ____.
e: After the particulate matter is removed by the electrostatic precipitator, the purified gas is vented.

q: In a scientific perspective, static electricity occurs when there is an imbalance of charges between two ____.
e: Static electricity is the result of an unequal distribution of electrons between materials.

q: Static electricity can build up as a result of collisions among the molecules in ____.
e: Friction and collisions between ice crystals and water droplets in clouds generate massive static charges.

q: This can cause a huge spark to form between the ground and the ____.
e: When the electric field becomes strong enough, it ionizes the air, creating a conductive path for a spark.

q: This causes a lightning discharge, therefore, a flow of charge through the ____.
e: Lightning is a massive, natural electrostatic discharge that equalizes the charge imbalance.

q: As aircraft fly through the air, they can become charged with static ____.
e: Friction with air molecules can cause a significant build-up of static charge on an aircraft's fuselage.

q: A build-up of static charge is a potential danger when refuelling aircraft or ____.
e: A static spark in the presence of fuel vapors can ignite them, causing a fire or explosion.

q: Fuel running through the pipes can provide the friction needed to create a static ____.
e: The flow of liquid fuel through hoses generates static electricity due to friction.

q: To prevent this, aircraft are earthed with a conductor during ____.
e: Earthing provides a safe path for the static charge to flow into the ground, preventing a spark.

q: Fuel tankers (bowsers) that transport fuel on roads must be earthed before any fuel is transferred, to prevent sparks causing a fire or ____.
e: Grounding the tanker ensures that any accumulated static charge is safely dissipated before fuel handling begins.

q: Television screen and computer monitors become charged with static electricity when they are ____.
e: The operation of electronic displays can generate a static charge on their outer surfaces.

q: These charges attract ____.
e: The static charge on the screen acts like a magnet for lightweight, neutral dust particles in the air.
